summary: Specifies the DOTS data channel, used for bulk exchange of data that cannot easily or appropriately be sent over the signal channel during an attack. It is the companion to the DOTS signal channel in RFC 8782.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network is under attack, there is a fast, small channel for saying 'I am being attacked'. This document describes the other channel: the slower one used to send the bigger, less urgent things, such as the list of addresses to block and the names the client will use for them later.

how does dots install filtering rules
subtitle: How a DDoS victim sends long-lived configuration, such as aliases and filtering rules, to its mitigation provider over RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: During a DDoS attack, the DOTS signal channel must stay small and robust, so it is a poor fit for bulk, infrequent data such as lists of prefixes and filtering rules.
tldr.mechanism: The DOTS data channel runs RESTCONF over TLS over TCP and defines a YANG module, 'ietf-dots-data-channel', that lets a DOTS client register itself, create aliases for protected resources, and install drop-list, accept-list and rate-limit rules on its DOTS server.
tldr.outcome: Clients get a reliable, authenticated way to manage aliases and filters ahead of and during an attack, with the signal channel referring to those aliases later. RFC 8783 is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8783 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the companion to the signal channel specification in RFC 8782.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DDoS attacks use many compromised end hosts to perpetrate and amplify an attack. The victim of such an attack can be an application server, a router, a firewall, or an entire network. The lack of a common method to coordinate a real-time response among the actors and network domains involved inhibits the speed and effectiveness of mitigation, and DOTS defines an architecture that allows a DOTS client to send requests to a DOTS server for DDoS attack mitigation.

DOTS defines two channels. The signal channel is used to carry information about a device or network, or a part of it, that is under attack. That information is sent by a DOTS client to an upstream DOTS server so that appropriate mitigation actions are undertaken on traffic deemed suspicious.

The data channel is used for infrequent bulk data exchange between DOTS agents, to significantly improve the coordination of all the parties involved in the response. It performs two tasks. The first is the creation of aliases for resources for which mitigation may be requested: a DOTS client may submit to its DOTS server a collection of prefixes that it would like to refer to by an alias when requesting mitigation, and the DOTS server responds with either a success or a failure response. The second task is policy management, which enables a DOTS client to request the installation or withdrawal of traffic filters, the dropping or rate-limiting of unwanted traffic, and the permitting of accept-listed traffic. A DOTS client is entitled to instruct filtering rules only on IP resources that belong to its own domain.

Two sample uses of drop- and accept-lists are given. If a network resource is informed about a potential attack from a set of IP addresses, the DOTS client informs its servicing DOTS gateway of all the suspect addresses that need to be drop-listed for further investigation, and could also specify a list of protocols and port numbers in the rule; the gateway then propagates the drop-listed addresses to a DOTS server, which takes action so that traffic from those addresses to the target network is blocked. Conversely, a network with partner sites from which only legitimate traffic arrives may want to ensure that traffic from those sites is not subjected to mitigation, and uses the data channel to convey the accept-listed prefixes of the partner sites, so that the server can accept-list flows from them.
sections.plainLanguage: One channel says 'I am under attack'. The other sends the bulkier material: the list of addresses to block, and the names to use for them later.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.content:
Unlike the signal channel, which must remain operational even when confronted with signal degradation due to packet loss, the data channel is not expected to be fully operational at all times, especially when an attack is underway. The specification does not require an order of signal and data channel creation, nor does it mandate a time interval between them; those are implementation and deployment specific.

As the primary function of the data channel is data exchange, a reliable transport mode is required so that DOTS agents can detect data delivery success or failure. The document uses RESTCONF over TLS over TCP as the data channel protocol, layered as DOTS Data Channel, RESTCONF, TLS, TCP and IP.

The HTTP POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE methods are used to edit data resources represented by the DOTS data channel YANG modules, which allow a DOTS client to alter the running configuration of the data channel. Configuration and state information can be retrieved with the GET method. An HTTP status line is returned for each request to report success or failure, and the error tag provides more information about encountered errors.

DOTS clients perform the root resource discovery procedure to determine the root of the RESTCONF API, and use that value as the initial part of the path in the request URI of any subsequent request. The server may support the retrieval of the YANG modules it supports, so a client may use RESTCONF to retrieve the vendor-specific YANG modules the server supports. JSON payloads are used to propagate the data-channel-specific payload messages that carry request parameters and response information, such as errors, using the encoding rules for representing YANG data as JSON text.

A DOTS client registers itself with its DOTS servers in order to set up data channel configuration data and to receive state data from them. A client can either maintain a persistent connection or initiate periodic connections. If the client needs to frequently update the drop-list or accept-list filtering rules or the aliases, it maintains a persistent connection. For example, a CAPTCHA or cryptographic puzzle can be used by the mitigation service in the client domain to determine whether an address is used for legitimate purposes, and the client can then frequently update the drop-list rules. A persistent connection is also useful if the client subscribes to event notifications. Clients SHOULD reuse the same TLS session to reduce workload, and may probe the server while the communication is quiescent to check it has kept its cryptographic state, which also keeps alive firewall and NAT bindings.

A DOTS server may detect conflicting filtering requests from distinct clients that belong to the same domain, for example one client asking to drop-list a prefix and another asking to accept-list the same source prefix with the same destination prefix. Servers SHOULD support a configuration parameter to indicate the behaviour to follow when a conflict is detected, such as rejecting all, rejecting the new request, or notifying an administrator. How a client synchronises its configuration with the server's is implementation specific: a client can systematically send a GET message before or after a configuration change request, or it can re-establish a disconnected session after an attack is mitigated and send a GET before the change request. The translation of filtering rules instantiated on a server into network configuration actions is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The data channel is ordinary web plumbing: RESTCONF requests over TLS, with JSON bodies and YANG as the model. The client registers once, then sends and fetches rules and aliases over that connection.

sections.title: Gateways and Loop Detection
sections.content:
When a server-domain DOTS gateway is involved in data channel exchanges, the same considerations for manipulating the 'cdid' parameter, the client domain identifier, must be followed by DOTS agents. That parameter assists the DOTS server in enforcing some policies, such as limiting the number of filtering rules per DOTS client or per client domain.

If a DOTS gateway is involved, the gateway verifies that the DOTS client is authorized to undertake a data channel action, for example instantiating filtering rules, and if the client is authorized the gateway propagates the rules to the upstream DOTS server. Likewise, the DOTS server verifies that the gateway is authorized to relay data channel actions. To create or purge filters, a client sends its request to its gateway, which validates the rules and proxies the request to the server; when the gateway receives the response it propagates it back to the client.

To detect and prevent infinite loops, DOTS gateways MUST support the loop-detection procedure of HTTP, and each intermediate gateway MUST check that none of its own information, such as server names or literal IP addresses, is present in the Via header field of a message it receives. If it detects its own information there, it MUST NOT forward the message; messages that cannot be forwarded because of a loop SHOULD be logged with a '508 Loop Detected' status line returned to the DOTS peer, and the reported error carries the error tag 'loop-detected', the error tag 'operation-failed', the error type 'transport, application', and a copy of the Via header field in the error info. Otherwise, the agent MUST update or insert the Via header field by appending its own information.

Unless configured otherwise, DOTS gateways at the boundaries of a client domain SHOULD remove the previous Via header field information after checking for a loop and before forwarding. This is required for topology hiding purposes and can also minimise conflicts that might arise if overlapping information, such as private IPv4 addresses or aliases that are not globally unique, is used in distinct DOTS domains.

A lifetime is associated with alias and filtering entries created by DOTS clients, to avoid stale entries, and DOTS servers may track the inactivity timeout of clients to detect them.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway in the middle checks that the client is allowed to ask for what it is asking for, and checks its own name in the message headers so that a forwarding loop is caught rather than run forever.

sections.title: Managing DOTS Clients
sections.content:
To make use of the data channel, a DOTS client MUST register with its DOTS servers by creating a 'dots-client' resource, and SHOULD do so with a POST request whose body carries a 'dots-client' list containing the 'cuid' parameter. The 'cuid' is a globally unique identifier meant to prevent collisions among DOTS clients, with the same meaning, syntax and processing rules as in the signal channel specification. It is a mandatory attribute, and clients MUST use the same 'cuid' for both the signal and the data channel.

In deployments where server-domain DOTS gateways are enabled, identity information about the origin source client domain SHOULD be supplied to the server, in the optional 'cdid' attribute, to assist the server in enforcing policies per client, per client domain, or both. The 'cdid' does not need to be inserted when relaying methods that manage aliases or filtering rules, because the servers are responsible for maintaining the association between 'cdid' and 'cuid' for policy enforcement purposes.

The server indicates the result of processing the POST request using status line codes: codes in the '2xx' range are success, '4xx' codes are some sort of invalid request, and '5xx' codes mean the server has erred or cannot accept the resource. In particular, '201 Created' is returned if the server has accepted the request, '400 Bad Request' is returned if the request does not include a 'cuid', with the error tag 'missing-attribute', and '409 Conflict' is returned if the data resource already exists, with the error tag 'resource-denied'. Servers MUST limit the number of 'dots-client' resources created by the same client to one per request, and MUST reject requests with multiple such resources.

Once a client has registered, it can create, delete and retrieve aliases and filtering rules. A client MAY use the PUT request to register instead. A client de-registers from its servers by deleting the 'cuid' resource, and resources bound to that client are deleted by the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The client registers once with a unique identifier of its own, which it must also use on the other channel. After that it can create and remove its rules.

sections.title: Managing DOTS Aliases
sections.content:
A POST or PUT request is used by a DOTS client to create aliases for resources for which a mitigation may be requested. Such aliases may be used in subsequent DOTS signal channel exchanges to refer more efficiently to the resources under attack. DOTS clients within the same domain can create different aliases for the same resource.

An alias carries a 'name', a list of 'target-prefix' values, a list of 'target-port-range' entries with a lower and an upper port, and a list of 'target-protocol' values. A DOTS server MUST maintain an alias for at least 10080 minutes, which is one week. If no refresh request is seen from the client, the server removes expired entries. A client uses the PUT request to modify its aliases, and in particular MUST update its alias entries upon change of the prefix indicated in the 'target-prefix'.

A GET request is used to retrieve one or all installed aliases. If no 'name' is included in the request, that indicates the request is about retrieving all the aliases instantiated by the client, and the 'content' query parameter selects the type of data requested.
sections.plainLanguage: An alias is a name the client gives to a group of addresses, ports and protocols, so that later it can say 'mitigate that one' on the fast channel instead of listing everything again.

sections.title: Managing DOTS Filtering Rules
sections.content:
A DOTS client MAY send a GET request to retrieve the filtering capabilities supported by its DOTS server, which reports the address families it supports, the forwarding actions, whether rate limiting is available, the transport protocol numbers, and which match criteria it supports for IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP and ICMP. A client that has issued such a request SHOULD NOT request filtering actions that the server does not support.

A POST or PUT request is used to communicate filtering rules. Each access list has a 'name', which is mandatory. It may have a 'type' indicating the primary intended type of match criteria, such as IPv4 or IPv6. The 'activation-type' indicates whether an access list has to be activated immediately or during mitigation time, or instantiated without being activated. Deactivated access lists can be activated later by manual configuration on the server or through the data channel. If the attribute is not provided, the server MUST use 'activate-when-mitigating' as the default. When a mitigation is in progress, the server MUST only activate 'activate-when-mitigating' filters that are bound to the client that triggered the mitigation.

The 'matches' element defines the criteria used to identify a flow to which the rule applies, and can be at layer 3, that is IPv4 or IPv6, or layer 4, that is TCP, UDP or ICMP. The destination prefix is mandatory in requests with an activation type of 'immediate', and servers MUST validate that these prefixes are within the scope of the DOTS client domain. If no destination prefix is given, the server enforces the access list on any destination address that belongs to the client domain. The 'actions' element carries a forwarding action of 'drop' or 'accept'; 'accept' is used to accept-list traffic and 'drop' to drop-list it. Accepted traffic may be subject to 'rate-limit', with the allowed rate in bytes per second.

The server reports the result of the POST with a status line: '201 Created' if the rules were accepted, '400 Bad Request' if a mandatory attribute is missing or a parameter is invalid or unknown, with the error tag set to 'missing-attribute', 'invalid-value' or 'unknown-element'. If the request arrives through a server-domain gateway and the server does not maintain a 'cdid' for that 'cuid' while one is expected, the server replies '403 Forbidden' with the error tag 'access-denied', and the client must then register. If the request conflicts with an existing filtering installed by another client of the domain and there is no local policy, the server returns '409 Conflict' with the error tag 'resource-denied'.

The client uses the PUT request to modify its filtering rules, and in particular MUST update its filtering entries upon change of the destination prefix. A server MUST maintain a filtering rule for at least 10080 minutes, which is one week, and removes expired entries if no refresh request is seen. Typically a refresh request is a PUT that echoes the content of a response to a GET request with all of the read-only parameters stripped out.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks what the server can do, then sends rules telling it to drop, accept or slow down traffic that matches given addresses and ports. The server reports back with a status line that says whether the rules were taken.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
DOTS servers MUST NOT enable both the DOTS data channel and direct configuration, to avoid race conditions and inconsistent configurations arising from simultaneous updates from multiple sources. DOTS agents SHOULD enable the data channel to configure aliases and access lists, and only use direct configuration as a stop-gap mechanism to test the signal channel with aliases and access lists; direct configuration should only be used when the on-path DOTS agents are within the same domain.

If a DOTS server has enabled direct configuration, it can reject the data channel connection using a hard ICMP error, or the reset bit in the TCP header, or reject the RESTCONF request using an error response containing a '503 Service Unavailable' status line.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick one way of configuring the server. Doing it both by hand and over the data channel at once leads to conflicting settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RESTCONF security considerations apply, and DOTS agents MUST support the mutual authentication TLS profile of the signal channel specification. Authenticated encryption MUST be used for data confidentiality and message integrity, so the interaction between the DOTS agents requires TLS with a cipher suite offering confidentiality protection.

Installing drop-list or accept-list rules over RESTCONF over TLS reveals the attacker addresses and the legitimate addresses only to the DOTS server trusted by the client. The secure channel provides privacy and prevents an eavesdropper from directly gaining access to those lists.

An attacker may be able to inject reset packets or bogus application segments regardless of whether TLS authentication is used. Because the application data is TLS protected, this will not result in the application receiving bogus data, but it constitutes a denial of service on the connection. The attack can be countered by using the TCP Authentication Option, where any bogus packets injected by an attacker are rejected by the integrity check and never reach the TLS layer.

To prevent leaking internal information outside a client domain, client-side DOTS gateways SHOULD NOT reveal the identity of internal DOTS clients, such as a source IP address or a client hostname, unless explicitly configured to do so. DOTS servers MUST verify that requesting clients are entitled to enforce filtering rules on a given IP prefix, so only filtering rules on resources that belong to the client domain can be authorised; the exact validation mechanism is deployment specific.

Rate-limiting DOTS requests, including those with new 'cuid' values, from the same client defends against denial-of-service attacks that would result from varying the identifier to exhaust server resources, and the rate-limit policies SHOULD be enforced on gateways if deployed and on servers. Applying a resource quota per client and per client domain, for example limiting the number of aliases and filters a client may install, prevents server resources from being aggressively used by some clients and ensures fairness in mitigation usage. Servers may also limit the number of clients that can be enabled per domain.

When fully qualified domain names are used as targets, the server MUST rely on DNS privacy enabling protocols, such as DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS, to prevent eavesdroppers from identifying the target resources protected by the service, and on authentic name resolution such as DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The channel is encrypted and both ends authenticate each other. The server must check that a client is only asking it to filter addresses the client is entitled to filter, and it should limit how many rules one client can install.

viz.caption: THE STATUS LINES A CLIENT MAY SEE (RFC 8783, SECTIONS 3.4, 5.1 AND 7.2)

items.label: Invalid request
items.desc: A mandatory attribute is missing, or a value is invalid or unknown.

items.label: Not authorised
items.desc: The server has no client domain identifier for this client.

items.label: No such resource
items.desc: The named access list is not installed for this client.

items.label: Conflict
items.desc: The resource already exists, or the request conflicts with another client's filtering.

items.label: Server refusing
items.desc: The server has enabled direct configuration and refuses the data channel.

items.label: Forwarding loop
items.desc: A gateway found its own information in the Via header field.

viz.caption: WHAT AN ALIAS IS FOR (RFC 8783, SECTION 6)

items.title: A short name for a group
items.text: The alias holds a list of target prefixes, port ranges and protocols.

items.title: Used on the fast channel
items.text: Later mitigation requests on the signal channel can refer to the resources by the alias instead of listing them again.

items.title: Refreshed or removed
items.text: The server keeps an alias for at least 10080 minutes, and removes it if no refresh request arrives.

items.title: Not shared between clients
items.text: Clients within the same domain can create different aliases for the same resource.
